title: Small Birds Stay Low
part: PART ONE: LIGHT WIND FROM THE WEST

pages.text:
*Sky Report: rising wind, gusty, a hedge full of opinions.*

The morning after the announcement, Thistlewick Hedge did not sleep. Instead, it buzzed, hummed, and argued. Two hundred sparrows woke up with news on their tongues, and the news was Pip.

Mother Wren, who had opinions on everything including the correct temperature for a sunbeam, hopped right up to Pip’s feet. "You should stick to worm-finding, dear," she said, preening a feather that did not need preening. "Worms are low. Worms are safe. Worms do not blow into next week."

The older fledglings, a pack of noisy chestnut and brown feathers, circled her. They hopped closer, leaning in with their beaks open in friendly, terrifying curiosity. "Too light," said one. "A sneeze and you’re gone," said another. "You’ll be blown right off the map," said a third, winking at his friend.

Pip stood on her twig, toes curled tight. She did not puff out her chest, nor did she shrink. Instead, she tilted her head, watching a leaf spin down from the highest branch.

"Tweet-truth?" she asked.

The birds stopped and blinked.

"Then I'll go there," she said, pointing her small beak at the distant, grey edge of the sky.
pages.image: A tiny brown-streaked sparrow with a crooked tail feather stands on a low branch, looking up at a group of larger, noisy sparrows perched on higher branches of a hedge, one pointing toward the sky.

pages.text:
Uncle Dorn found her behind the honeysuckle, where the green grew thick and the light stayed dim. He was ruffled. His plumage looked like a storm cloud that had been sat on, and the grey in his feathers seemed paler than usual.

He did not grumble. He did not say she was the smallest. Instead, he looked at the sky, which was very blue and very far away, then down at Pip, who was very small and very close.

"The wind is too rough," he said. His voice was thin, stripped of its usual grumbly bulk. "The sky is too big. And the Storm-Sparrows are the ones who don't come back."

Pip had never seen him afraid. It was a strange feeling, like hearing a thunderclap in a quiet room. He extended his wing, not to hold her, but to block the breeze.

"Small birds stay low," he said, more gently than he had ever spoken in her eleven weeks of life. "Low is safe."

Pip looked at his soft, trembling feathers. Then she looked at the sky, which was not listening.

"Low is small," she said.

She was surprised at herself. The words had not been planned. They had just fallen out, light as dandelion seeds, into the quiet space between them.
pages.image: A plump, gloomy grey sparrow with ruffled feathers hovers protectively near a tiny sparrow with a crooked tail, both facing a bright, open blue sky above a dense honeysuckle bush.

pages.text:
Elder Marra was already waiting on the Gathering Rock, her torn wing tip flaring like a jagged flag in the breeze. She did not look up when Pip landed on the rough stone three feet away, though the elder’s dark eyes shifted to acknowledge the new weight.

"I'm entering the Trial," Pip said.

Marra’s head cocked. One sharp eye slid sideways to look at Pip directly, while the other stayed fixed on the horizon. "You weigh less than a walnut," Marra said. Her voice was not loud, but it filled the space between them like a heavy stone dropped into a quiet room.

"I can fly," Pip replied.

Marra shifted her weight, and the stone crunched under her claws. "The Trial is not for chicks who are too light to be caught by the wind. It is for birds who can steer it." She turned her head fully, fixing Pip with a gaze that felt like being checked for homework. "Storm-Sparrows are built, not wished."

It was not unkind. It was worse than unkind. It was certain, a door closing smooth and final. Pip’s chest went tight, a drum skin pulled so high it might snap. She wanted to argue, to point to the sky, to do a loop. But she just stood there, small and brown, while Marra turned back to the horizon and said nothing more.
pages.image: A large, grey-streaked elder sparrow with a torn wing tip sits on a rocky outcrop, looking down at a tiny, round sparrow standing on the stone below, with a vast, empty sky behind them.

pages.text:
At the seed patch, the air smelled of dust and dried sun, and Cinder was there, glossy chestnut preening a wing with the serious concentration of a painter mixing colors. He heard the news before Pip even reached the center.

"Pip? In the Trial?"

He laughed. It was a short, dry sound, like a twig snapping, and then he spread his wings, wide and powerful, to catch an updraft. He did not just fly; he soared. He banked, tilted, and rolled, a perfect barrel roll that left a ghost of motion in the air.

The other fledglings watched, beaks open, eyes wide. They whispered. *Look at him. Look at the speed. Look at the grace.*

Cinder landed, dusting off his feathers. "The wind would take you off like a dandelion seed," he said, shaking his head. "Tweet-truth, you should hold on to a twig and pray."

Pip watched him land. She did not sneer. She did not pout. Instead, she watched the way his tail feather acted as a rudder, and the way his wings flexed at the very last second to catch the drop. She memorized it. Every angle. Every beat. It was the best barrel roll she had ever seen, and she was going to learn exactly how it worked.
pages.image: A glossy chestnut sparrow performs an aerial barrel roll above a sunny seed patch, while a tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail watches intently from the ground, surrounded by other sparrows.

pages.text:
Night settled over Thistlewick Hedge, thick and quiet, before the stars emerged. They brightened the darkness, looking like a handful of dropped peppermints. Pip tucked her head under her wing in the deepest knot of thorns. The twigs tangled there like knotted shoelaces.

A shadow shifted in the leaves. Nettle landed, her large feet silent on the dried grass. She sat close enough for Pip to feel the gentle warmth of her small body. Nettle did not speak at once. She just waited, watching the sky.

"Everyone says you can't," Nettle whispered, her voice barely a breath against the night air. She looked up, her eyes wide and dark. "Do you think you can?"

Pip lifted her head. The sky above was vast and black, stitched with pinpricks of light. It felt terrifying. It felt beautiful. It felt like it was waiting.

She did not answer right away. She watched the stars until her eyes ached. The night stopped feeling like a heavy blanket and started feeling like a door.

"I don't know," she said finally. "But I know I can't if I don't try. And that's the only thing that's true for sure."
pages.image: Two small sparrows, one tiny with a crooked tail and one skinny with large feet, huddle together in the dark shadows of a hedge, looking up at a starry night sky.
